title: 4 Chip Stocks Down as Much as 36% From Their Highs to Buy and Hold for the Next Decade

4 Chip Stocks Down as Much as 36% From Their Highs to Buy and Hold for the Next Decade
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Mon, November 16, 2026 at 5:01 PM CST 6 min read
AMD
MU
TSM
ASML
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Most chip stocks are far off their highs. As I write, Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) trades around 18% below its record close, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM) sits about 18% below its own. ASML (NASDAQ:ASML) is about 25% under its June record, and Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) is about 36% under its own.

Each handles a different link in the chain that turns artificial intelligence (AI) spending into hardware. AMD designs chips. TSMC makes them, partly using ASML's lithography machines (which print a chip's patterns on silicon wafers). And Micron provides the memory that sits next to them.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

For a 10-year hold, I think this matters. Some of these companies get paid almost no matter whose chip wins. Others have to keep winning.

Image source: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company.

1. AMD's data center sales are accelerating

AMD's data center segment sells server processors and AI chips. Showing how fast this business is scaling, its revenue climbed 97% year over year in the third quarter to a record $8.5 billion, up from $6.7 billion in the second quarter and $5.8 billion in the first. Growth from the previous quarter accelerated from 16% to 27%. And the segment now makes up 64% of AMD's sales, up from 47% a year earlier.

That's well above the more than 60% a year AMD targets for the segment over the next three to five years.

The biggest risk, I think, is the price. At around $535, AMD trades at about 30 times the earnings analysts expect for 2027. Even its own target of adjusted earnings over $20 a share in three to five years puts today's price at about 27 times those earnings.

2. TSMC just had its best month ever

AMD depends on TSMC for all its processor and graphics chip wafers at 7 nanometers or less (a lower number means a more advanced chip), according to AMD's last quarterly filing.

Notably, chips built at 7 nanometers or below brought in 79% of TSMC's wafer revenue in the third quarter, as total revenue grew 41% year over year in U.S. dollars and net income climbed 69% in Taiwan dollars. Then October's sales set a monthly record of around 587 billion Taiwan dollars, up about 60% from a year earlier.

Of course, most of TSMC's main plants are in Taiwan. A conflict or trade fight involving the island is the biggest risk, because it might disrupt the factories AMD relies on.

International Business Machines recently announced a series of quantum and AI moves, including new Nighthawk processors, a Chicago Quantum System Two deployment, multiple co-design platforms with partners such as NVIDIA, AMD, Fermilab, and Oak Ridge, and an AI agent platform collaboration with Microsoft.

These projects point to IBM leaning heavily into capital-intensive, research-heavy quantum and enterprise AI infrastructure. This could influence long-term margins, required investment, and how its Software, Consulting, and Infrastructure segments work together in practice.

The next area of focus will be how IBM's existing hybrid cloud and AI investment narrative aligns with its quantum co-design initiatives with NVIDIA.

Spot 53 AI infrastructure stocks that, like IBM, are pouring resources into quantum-ready AI hardware and enterprise platforms before this buildout phase matures.

International Business Machines Investment Narrative Recap

To own International Business Machines, you need to believe its shift toward hybrid cloud, AI and now quantum-ready infrastructure can keep earnings and cash flow resilient while growth stays moderate. Recent quantum and AI partnerships, plus the new Nighthawk roadmap, keep that thesis focused on Software and Consulting execution rather than one-off hardware wins.

The immediate catalyst is how quickly IBM converts its reported generative AI book of business into higher margin Software revenue and stable free cash flow. The recent yen fixed-income deals look incremental. They tweak funding and interest costs but do not materially change the near term risk, which still centers on high debt and execution in AI.

The IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 and r3 announcements look most relevant to this buildout. They sit right where the story is heading, toward quantum-ready AI infrastructure that leans on IBM Quantum Platform, classical supercomputing tie-ins, and a growing ecosystem across partners like Oak Ridge and AMD.

For you as a shareholder, the key issue is how effectively IBM turns that technical roadmap into commercial Software and Consulting projects that support margins while also funding capital-intensive quantum work. Execution on this front will likely matter more to the catalyst than funding mechanics. At the same time, the existing high debt load still depends on consistent free cash flow to remain manageable.

On kapirey's numbers, the narrative reaches a fair value of US$256.08 by applying a discounted cash flow style framework that assumes IBM can compound revenue at 6.0% a year and eventually sustain an 18.0% profit margin on that higher sales base.

title: Is AMD Stock Still a Buy After Its Post-Earnings Jump?
detail:
Is AMD Stock Still a Buy After Its Post-Earnings Jump?
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool
Mon, November 16, 2026 at 3:43 PM CST 5 min read
AMD
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) investors have been on quite the roller-coaster ride since it reported Q3 earnings on Nov. 3. While the initial reaction to its earnings was fairly muted, the stock sold off along with the market shortly after its results came out and was down over 15% at one point.

Then AMD got a second catalyst for change: On Nov. 9, the stock surged 13.3% on news that Google Cloud selected its fifth-generation EPYC processors for the TPU 8tx platform. As a result, Oppenheimer upgraded AMD's rating to Outperform.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

That was followed later in the week by a third catalyst: Big trouble at its primary competitor, Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA).

Image source: Getty Images.

Last week, Nvidia's CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned amid misconduct allegations, and with its primary competitor now without its visionary leader, AMD's stock rose. While the rise peaked at about 20%, up from the level it entered earnings at, it's now about equal its pre-earnings price on recent general market turmoil.

The question is, is AMD still a buy at these levels, or have these catalysts drastically affected the AMD investment thesis? Let's take a look, as investors need to consider multiple factors before investing in AMD.

AMD's gains may not be immediate

Let's take a look at AMD's Q3 results, since that occurred first in the timeline. During Q3, AMD's overall revenue rose 45% year over year to $13.4 billion. Its data center business rose 97% year over year to $8.5 billion, showcasing strong demand in the most important computing sector. While it also has other business units, what investors really care about is the data center division, as it's the biggest growth area right now.

Nvidia has a huge market-share lead in this sector, and it will be difficult for AMD to catch up. But with a new leader coming in at Nvidia, will this potentially allow it to close the gap? I don't think so.

The reality is that Nvidia's products and ecosystem are better than AMD's right now. Furthermore, switching from one computing unit provider to another isn't easy. Additionally, while Jensen Huang was leading the company, he couldn't do everything. He had a talented team working for him, and those people are largely still in place.

The next few years of development are still in place; the question is what comes after that. That will determine how AMD fares against Nvidia in the three-to-five-year time frame, and depending on who is selected to replace Huang, it could inform whether AMD looks like a better long-term investment option.

Huang's Exit and Comeback Reports Shake NVIDIA Before Earnings

NVIDIA announced on November 12 that Huang was stepping down as CEO of the chipmaker he co-founded, and finance chief Colette Kress was named interim CEO. Huang's departure followed reports about his personal conduct, including China-related allegations that remain unverified. Huang denied that he had compromised national security or company secrets.
